newsitem.title: INDIA: INDIAN BANKS-Technology vs labour in public sector.
newsitem.headline: INDIAN BANKS-Technology vs labour in public sector.

text.p: India's state-controlled banks need to upgrade technology in order to face the challenge from more efficient private domestic and foreign banks but worker resistance is holding them back, analysts said on Wednesday.
"Labour resistance to change is the biggest disadvantage that public sector banks face in their attempts to upgrade technology," said Prasanna Marar, banking analyst at Mafatlal Securities in Bombay.
"Upgrading (technology) is essential if state-run banks are to improve services and efficiency and tackle the challenge from private and foreign banks," Marar said.
Financial sector reforms started in the early 1990s have thrown up a host of new opportunities for public sector banks but they have also increased competition.
Public sector banks dominate India's banking industry with 80 percent of total bank deposits and 78 percent of advances as of March 31, 1997.
But their levels of efficiency are well below those of other classes of banks according to the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) latest report on the trend and progress of banking.
Operating profits of new private sector banks, started since 1994, were 2.8 percent of total assets and of older private banks 2.3 percent. It was 3.3 percent for foreign banks.
For public-sector banks, operational profits were only 1.1 percent of total assets, with the State Bank of India (SBI) and its seven fully owned associates recording 2.1 percent.
"With financial sector deregulation, competition is increasing and spreads are falling," Marar said.
"Public sector banks will have to raise productivity and technology will play a vital role in ensuring this," she said.
Public sector bankers said improved technology is one way in which performance can be improved.
But so far there has only been mechanisation, they said.
"Actually, there has been little technology introduced in public sector banks," said an economist at a state-run bank.
"If you look at the computers introduced in our (public sector) banks, they are little more than electronic typing machines or adding machines. We are not allowed to really computerise."
Agreements between trade unions and bank managements specify the level of technology to be used in public sector banks.
Analysts say that these agreements have effectively neutralised the effects of computerisation.
"I think labour resistance to technology was quite strong in the early years (of reforms)," said Sandeep Nanda, banking analyst at NatWest Markets.
"So banks initially went in for lower technology and mainly back-office computerisation," Nanda said.
"Now the problem is one of networking and integrating the older and newer technologies," he said.
Unions however deny they are against technology.
"It is not true to say that we are against technology," said Tarakeshwar Chakraborthy, general secretary of the All India Bank Employees Association (AIBEA), the industry's largest union.
"As per the agreement signed with the bank managements in October 1993, we have given almost complete freedom to banks."
He said unions had not imposed restrictions.
"We are only against computerisation in small branches where the number of vouchers is less or in rural areas where transactions are mainly cash-based," Chakraborthy said.
"The real problem is that bank managements do not understand technology and are proceeding in a haphazard manner."

The unions flexed their muscles last month with one-day strike to protest the setting up of new private banks in rural areas, as well as wage issues and the implementation of a pension plan in private banks. About 1.3 million employees stayed away from work, crippling banking operations across the country.
Bank unions plan a two-day strike on August 28-29 to press their demands.
